title: Current Mirrors
intro: A current mirror copies a reference current to another branch. Mirrors are used for biasing and as active loads throughout analog circuits.

blocks.text: Two NMOS transistors share the same VGS: M1 is diode-connected and carries the reference current Iref. M2 has the same gate and source voltages, so ideally

Errors come from channel-length modulation (VDS1 = VGS differs from VDS2 = Vout, giving Iout/Iref = [(W/L)2/(W/L)1] * (1 + lambda*VDS2)/(1 + lambda*VDS1)), from threshold and geometry mismatch, and from short-channel effects. Use long channels to reduce lambda.

Add a cascode device on top of each branch. The output resistance becomes about gm*ro^2 (versus ro), so the output current is almost independent of Vout. The cost is headroom: the minimum output voltage rises from Vov to VTH + 2*Vov. A 'wide-swing' cascode bias reduces this to about 2*Vov.

Try raising lambda: the basic mirror's current climbs with Vout and rises above the ideal line, while the cascode mirror stays flat once it has its headroom. Lower Vov to see the cascode working at lower voltages.

blocks.title: Mirror error from lambda
blocks.text: Iref = 100 uA, ratio (W/L)2/(W/L)1 = 2, lambda = 0.1 V^-1, VGS = 0.7 V (so VDS1 = 0.7 V), Vout = 1.2 V. Find Iout.

blocks.title: Cascode output resistance
blocks.text: gm = 1 mS and ro = 50 kohm in both devices of a cascode mirror. Roughly how much does Iout change when Vout moves by 1 V in the basic and cascode mirror?
solution: Basic: Rout = ro = 50 kohm, so Delta-I = 1 V / 50 kohm = 20 uA.
Cascode: Rout is about (1 + gm*ro)*ro = 51 * 50 kohm = 2.55 Mohm, so Delta-I = 0.39 uA, over 50 times less.
